analysis.one_liner: Bars private contractors from interrogating or detaining US-held prisoners and requires intelligence agencies to report contractor spending.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in House committees from February 2009 until Congress ended in January 2011, with no hearing or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would forbid private companies from carrying out arrests, interrogations, detentions, and prisoner transfers for the US government — work done by government employees instead. It would also force intelligence agencies to tell Congress each year how many contractors they hire, what those contractors do, how much they cost, which contractors have been investigated for possible crimes, and how many foreign nationals they employ. The aim was to close a gap exposed by abuses at Abu Ghraib and CIA 'black site' detentions, where private interrogators answered to companies rather than to the public.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens gain in two ways. First, people taken into US custody abroad could no longer be interrogated or detained by private companies whose personnel were not subject to military or civilian government discipline — the situation that produced documented abuses at Abu Ghraib, where contractor interrogators were involved. Second, taxpayers gain because Congress would finally see, in one annual report per agency, how many intelligence contractors are being paid, what they cost, and which ones are under criminal investigation. Government employees who do the same work for less would also benefit from required plans to convert contractor jobs into government jobs.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits private contractors from arresting, interrogating, detaining, or transporting prisoners in US custody, with a six-month deadline for compliance [S3].
Exempts only language interpreters working under direct government supervision, so the ban targets companies performing coercive custody functions [S3].

Requires the Director of National Intelligence to file an annual assessment for each intelligence agency showing contractor headcount, costs, trends over five years, and a list of every contractor under Inspector General or criminal investigation, submitted to the intelligence committees [S3].

Requires every covered intelligence contract over $1 million to disclose personnel training, hiring and background-check processes, numbers of foreign nationals, and itemized cost estimates and actual costs [S3].

Requires a report to Congress on contractor-performed intelligence collection, analysis, covert action, and surveillance of US citizens, including cost comparisons with government employees and plans to convert contractor positions into government employment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Intelligence contractors would lose the most lucrative and least-scrutinized part of their business: interrogation and detention work. Intelligence agencies would bear administrative costs of annual reporting and of hiring government employees to replace contractor personnel, which could cost more in salary and benefits even as it improves accountability.

drawbacks.text: The bill acknowledges intelligence agencies already rely heavily on contractors; replacing contract interrogators and support staff with government employees would require hiring, training, and security-clearance costs, and agencies argued (in the broader post-2009 debate on intelligence insourcing) that contractors provide flexibility for surge operations.

The annual assessments and contract disclosures would be submitted to the intelligence committees, not the public, and the main report would be unclassified only 'in form' with a classified annex, so the transparency gains were limited to congressional oversight [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability and civil-liberties gains — taking coercive custody functions out of private hands and giving Congress real numbers on contractor use — outweigh the compliance costs, which are the routine cost of oversight. The main design limitation is that the added transparency runs to Congress rather than to the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees when introduced, one of them referred it to a subcommittee four months later, and then nothing happened — no hearing, no vote — until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Price (D-NC) introduced the bill on February 10, 2009, joined by seven original cosponsors [S3].
The House referred it to three committees the same day: Intelligence (Permanent Select), Armed Services, and Judiciary [S5].
On July 23, 2009, the Judiciary Committee referred it to its Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties [S5].
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a committee vote, a hearing, or a floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].
Twelve House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Intelligence contractors and the agencies that employ them are better off: they kept interrogation and detention work in private hands and avoided new annual reporting on contractor numbers, costs, and investigations. Members of Congress also avoided having to take a recorded vote on a politically sensitive national-security measure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Intelligence contractors and the agencies hiring them

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on [S4], but no committee or floor vote was ever held, so the actual partisan divide was never tested.

industries.note: The bill bans contractors from arrest, interrogation, detention, and prisoner transfer — the most sensitive work in this market — and subjects all intelligence contracts over $1 million to personnel, cost, and investigation disclosures. These companies profited from work performed outside normal government accountability; the bill would have ended that arrangement. [S3]
Explicitly exempted from the prohibition so long as interpreters work under direct government supervision, so this segment could continue serving detention operations. [S3]
